To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of national PPPs to deflate GDP at the regional level can lead to misleading results about regional convergence and the effectiveness of Structural Funds.

the use of national PPPs to deflate regional GDPs is likely to be misleading, particularly when regional differences in the cost of living are large, and that a system of regional purchasing power parites would be a valuable tool to inform EU policy.

the use of national purchasing power parities (PPP) to deflate regional Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in order to derive comparable regional GDP figures is likely to lead to a systematic underestimation of regional GDP.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a set of regional PPPs which would allow regional GDP to be deflated by regional prices.
the development of a set of European regional PPPs for use in regional policy and analysis.
how regional PPPs might best be estimated, and what the likely impact of such an approach would be on our current understanding of regional convergence.

there is a clear case for the development of a regional PPP system, and it should be developed as soon as possible.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the development of regional PPPs is feasible, and could be of considerable value to policy-makers, particularly in the evaluation of Structural Fund programmes, but also in the assessment of other EU programmes.
there are many challenges to overcome in order to produce a system of regional purchasing power parites, but that the potential benefits for EU policy would be significant.
there is much work still to be done before a robust system of regional PPP can be developed, and that it will require significant resources and time to develop.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there are significant differences in prices between regions in the Member States, and that the use of national price data is likely to lead to an overstatement of the level of GDP per capita in some regions and an understatement in other regions.

there are significant differences between national and regional prices, and that these differences are large enough to affect the conclusions made about regional development and the effectiveness of Structural Funds.

regional price differences are significant and that they are not captured in current estimates of GDP at regional level, and that the implications for policy are likely to be important, particularly for the Structural Funds and for the conclusions made so far about the convergence of regions.
